title: Following One Atom Through the Cell

scenes.tts: Which molecule is made first? Where does part of a virus end up? Are the proteins of the body replaced? These are questions about the fate of atoms, not about amounts. The answer is the isotope trick. Feed a labelled compound A. Later isolate a labelled compound B. Then the conversion of A to B is established.
scenes.visual: A big row: three question panels (which molecule first, where a virus part ends up, are body proteins replaced) appear as asked; 'amounts' is struck out beside 'fate of atoms'; then compound A with a label dot, an unknown path of question marks, and compound B with a label dot.
scenes.narration: Which molecule is made first? Where does part of a virus end up? Are the proteins of the body replaced? These are questions about the fate of atoms, not about amounts. The answer is the isotope trick. Feed a labelled compound A. Later isolate a labelled compound B. Then the conversion of A to B is established.

scenes.tts: Pick an isotope of an element the molecule contains. It can be radioactive, like carbon fourteen or phosphorus thirty-two. Or it can be stable and heavy, like nitrogen fifteen. The cell should treat the labelled molecule like the natural one. Deuterium-labelled metabolites were essentially indistinguishable from natural ones by the methods then used, yet could still be traced.
scenes.visual: A compound chip with one marker swapped for a radioactive (yellow, rays) or a stable heavy (purple, large) version; natural and labelled chips enter one cell the same way; a blue detector tells them apart.
scenes.caption: Pick an isotope of an element the molecule contains. It can be radioactive, like carbon-14 or phosphorus-32. Or it can be stable and heavy, like nitrogen-15. scenes.tts: Feed the labelled compound, or grow cells on it. Then stop the cells quickly at set times. Calvin's group fed algae carbon dioxide containing carbon fourteen. They took samples after short exposures and dropped them into hot methanol, which stopped all enzyme reactions. Then they separated the products on two-dimensional paper chromatography.
scenes.visual: Flask of algae fed labelled CO2; a time axis with sample times; each sample drops into hot methanol (reactions stop); then a big paper sheet with solvent arrows along two edges and labelled spots spreading out.
scenes.caption: Feed the labelled compound, or grow cells on it. Then stop the cells quickly at set times. Calvin's group fed algae carbon dioxide containing carbon-14. scenes.tts: Now find the label. Radioactive decay gives off radiation. Lay the paper on X-ray film, and each labelled spot darkens the developed film. Or count the label in a purified fraction with a scintillation counter. A stable isotope is found by its mass. Nitrogen fifteen was measured by turning a sample's nitrogen into N two gas and comparing mass twenty-eight with mass twenty-nine in a mass spectrometer.
scenes.visual: Three readouts: paper on film with spots darkening; a purified fraction into a counter with a rising count; a mass spectrometer with two peaks at mass 28 and 29 (example).

scenes.tts: A dark spot or a high count means label arrived there. Its intensity tracks how much label, not how much of the molecule in total. Here is Shemin, who took nitrogen fifteen glycine for three days. The label in heme rose to a maximum, stayed nearly level for months, then fell. That gave a red cell life span of about one hundred twenty-seven days.
scenes.visual: A film strip of spots (darker = more label) with the note; then a time plot (idealised from the reported timings): rise to a maximum at about 20 days, level for 80 days, then fall; result chip: red-cell life span 127 days.
scenes.caption: A dark spot or a high count means label arrived there. Its intensity tracks how much label, not how much of the molecule in total. scenes.tts: A label marks anything that takes it up. Hokin and Hokin tried to follow phosphorus thirty-two into RNA, but the counts kept vanishing in purification. The discarded material was phospholipid. So identify the labelled compound; do not guess it from where the label shows up. And half-life is part of the design. Phosphorus thirty-two loses half its activity in about fourteen days.
scenes.visual: Left: label expected in RNA, counts vanish in purification, the discard pile holds phospholipid; control: analyse the discard, identify the compound. Right: an idealised decay curve with a half-life marker.

scenes.tts: Calvin, Benson and Bassham, at Berkeley, fed algae carbon dioxide containing carbon fourteen. In a fraction of a second, most of the labelled carbon was in three-phosphoglyceric acid, the first stable product of carbon dioxide fixation. A short pulse of label shows which products appear first. Schoenheimer and Rittenberg, from 1935, found that many body constituents are in constant renewal. Only a label tells new molecules from old ones of the same kind.
scenes.visual: Two rows. Row 1: pulse timeline, 3-phosphoglyceric acid spot appears first, later spots after (Calvin, Benson, Bassham, Berkeley, late 1940s to 1953). Row 2: a body of grey chips gradually replaced by labelled ones (Schoenheimer and Rittenberg, from 1935).

scenes.tts: Hershey and Chase, in 1952, tracked the two parts of one virus separately. Sulfur thirty-five marks protein. Phosphorus thirty-two ends up mostly in DNA. Most phage DNA entered the bacterium. Most of the sulfur-containing coat stayed outside. The cells still made phage. The authors warned against drawing further chemical inferences. Keep this rule. A label shows where atoms went. Identify the compound before you conclude.
scenes.visual: A phage as two labelled chips (protein coat with sulfur-35, DNA mostly with phosphorus-32); the DNA moves into a bacterium and the coat stays outside; new phage emerge; the rule box (Hershey and Chase, 1952).
